items.title: Everything changed for the oil, AI and bond trades over the past month
items.summary: The market expects oil to keep rising, but treasury yields have declined, a warning traders and investors may be more worried about an AI crash than inflation.
items.content:
How everything changed for the oil, AI and bond trades in October
Oil futures have risen over the past month, but breaking with what had been an 80% correlation this year, treasury yields declined during the same time period.
What changed? The decline in the leading artificial intelligence stocks, the Mag 7, according to Jeffrey Rosenberg, senior portfolio manager of the Systematic Alternatives ETF at the world's largest asset manager, BlackRock, speaking on the most recent CNBC "ETF Edge."
"Oil and treasury yields had this amazing correlation and in October it just stopped," he said. "It told us something important. In the market's mind, the geopolitical risk is secondary to AI risk."
If there was one safe bet over the course of 2026, it was that treasury yields would rise alongside a move up in oil futures contracts. Over the past month, that ended, and according to Jeffrey Rosenberg, senior portfolio manager of the Systematic Alternatives ETF ( IALT ) at BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, the breakdown in that trade has big implications for the market.
"Oil and treasury yields had this amazing correlation and in October it just stopped," Rosenberg said on the most recent CNBC "ETF Edge."
The relationship between oil and bond yields was featured in Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's FOMC press conference on Wednesday, with Warsh noting how oil futures have continued to rise, a factor the central bank must consider in its fight against inflation. But Rosenberg said what Warsh didn't talk about was "the most important takeaway."
"Treasuries and oil had an 80% correlation this year," Rosenberg said, which is "outsize" relative to normal correlations. "We've basically been trading off oil for good reason." "
What happened? Rosenberg says you can sum it up by looking to the deflated AI trade. As the market moved away from that oil-treasuries trading correlation in October, "It told us something important," he said. "In the market's mind, the geopolitical risk is secondary to AI risk," he said.
Over the past month — which became most painfully clear in Friday's Nasdaq market wipeout and, earlier the week, Google's biggest single-day decline in its history, wiping out half a trillion dollars in value — the AI trade experienced a retracement. Bond yields went lower, Rosenberg says, because the market is equating weakness in the AI trade as a broader weakness in the U.S. economy. And he said, last week's GDP report backed up that thinking. "AI is everything, everywhere, all the time," he said. Both the growth for the economy on the investment side and the wealth effect on the consumption side are all AI, he said.
"Q3 GDP was a blowout [number] and all AI-related," Rosenberg said on the "ETF Edge" podcast extended conversation . He pointed to equipment investment increases and consumption well above expectations and both fueled by the AI wealth effect, which with the latter is even more notable given that real incomes have been coming down in the U.S.
Business investment of 12.7% in Q3 was the biggest increase outside the pandemic since 2011, led by a 37% rise in information processing equipment. Industrial equipment investment rose nearly 25%, which while not a straight AI trade, does partially reflect spending on data centers.
Magnificent Seven ETF performance over the past month.
Warsh did not agree in his assessment of the economy at the FOMC press conference. "It is convenient to say that the strength of the economy is all about this new technology wave. In fact, if we look at the data, really including data from the last meeting until this, the capex story is not just robust, not just strong, but it is broadening. And so if you wanted to tell the story somehow that this is strength we're seeing only in narrow pockets, that's a much harder story to tell now than it would have been several quarters ago," he said.
But Rosenberg says that's not a conclusion that the October market came to and it all adds up to a situation in which he says any "wobble" in the AI trade is going to be seen as a wobble in the growth outlook for the U.S., and as disinflationary. And in a disinflationary environment, there is "only one thing that hedges," he said, and that is "the thing everyone wants to hate. ... the long end of the treasury curve."
"That's the really important lesson from last month of market performance," he said.
U.S. 10-year treasury yield performance over the past month.
Despite this view, Rosenberg is cautious about suggesting that this dynamic makes bonds a safe bet. "The simple answer is it's not a return to normal, where normal was bonds hedging stocks," he said.
That is because of the conflicting forces on bonds. Oil price increases and the persistent level of inflation above target are not going away as challenges to fixed-income assets and the "efficacy," Rosenberg said, of fixed income as a hedge.
"There's too much inflation and that limits the ability of the Fed to provide accommodation, and we haven't gotten away from that," he said. "But what we've learned in the last month is if it's big enough, if the AI trend turns against the macroeconomy and inflationary trends, it can bring about a wholesale change in that direction that's disinflationary and bonds may react like they did in October," he said.
Still, he says investors should not bet the trade will be one-directional or come without a potential cost. Investors need to weigh the potential diversification benefit from bonds based on the October action versus a scenario in which AI does not unravel the economy. And the longer the AI boom persists, coupled with the broader fiscal challenges in the U.S., "bonds will be challenged," he said.
The AI trade itself is a very big piece of the bond market, and that showed up over the past week in a major way between both the Google earnings decline and Microsoft coming back into the public bond market. "It was a surprise to the markets. It hadn't been back in close to a decade," Rosenberg said.
As the capex needs of the tech giants begin to overwhelm their free cash flow more regularly, the public bond markets are coming to terms with an expected flood of issuance . "When the bonds markets, the public bond markets, look at where it is all coming from ... it's a huge marginal issuer, and its increasingly all coming again and again," he said.
The hyperscalers are reaching the limits of the financing that bank loan and private credit markets can offer and while Rosenberg stressed that a $40 trillion to $60 trillion global bond market can absorb an expected $4 trillion in AI debt over the next four years, "the market is not unlimited in capacity."
That demand will lead to lower prices and higher spreads, though Microsoft's deal attracted huge investor interest and was oversubscribed.
Rosenberg said it's a good thing that more of the hyperscale debt is being pushed into the public bond market because it means there will be more transparency in the form of bond prices and CDS spreads. While spreads on Microsoft credit default swaps are currently trading near a five-year high, roughly 55, they are still a world away from Oracle CDS spreads, by comparison, which are closer to 300. That presents another trading opportunity for investors who may not want to buy bonds outright given the inflationary environment and fiscal challenges in the U.S., but may still be looking for ways to hedge bets on the AI boom.
"That old tool from the Great Financial Crisis," he said. "Short it. You can trade two ways in [public] credit markets and you can't do that in bank loans and private credit. But once they start going in public markets, you can do that."
Rosenberg said a 12% down day in Google is "not even on the chart" historically. "So it's moving into a different zip code, if you will, of market pricing and market volatility and market indigestion. It's not the end of the world, it's just a different world of the AI buildout," he said, with the greater transparency in the public bond market giving investors more ability to trade "the emotional swings between fear and greed," he said.
What the CDS market is telling investors with the large-cap hyperscaler names, according to Rosenberg, is not that the prospect of default is high, but that as all the companies try to access more debt financing, the capacity of the banks and financial intermediaries to find counter-parties for the risk is becoming more limited.
"Think about financial markets and these big investment booms. They don't move in one direction. They ratchet up, reset." But with the AI boom, it's only been "the positive part," Rosenberg said. "It's still an incredibly positive story, but you get a little of the balance with the AI pessimism."

The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Donald Trump ’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.
The port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires
The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.
Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.
By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.
China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.
A girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026. Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/Reuters It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions . While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.
Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.
China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions , covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.
One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.
Workers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China. Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty Images China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.
This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?
The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

Rubio Casts Doubts On Quick Deal To End War In Ukraine, Defends Russian Contacts
Rubio Casts Doubts On Quick Deal To End War In Ukraine, Defends Russian Contacts
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Atlanta on October 31: Not 'claiming that we're on the verge of a negotiated settlement.'
ATLANTA, Georgia -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was unsure whether a negotiated end to the war in Ukraine was possible, while European officials told RFE/RL the top US diplomat also privately expressed doubts that Russian President Vladimir Putin would attend December's Miami G20 summit.
The European officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Rubio also privately shared his doubts with Western counterparts of a peace deal in the coming months during the two days of G20 foreign ministers' talks in Atlanta, which wrapped up on October 31.
Rubio's public remarks at his closing news conference were notably cautious. Asked by RFE/RL whether he believed a negotiated settlement was achievable given Moscow's unchanged position, he said Washington was still trying to establish whether an agreement could be reached.
"I don't know if negotiated peace is achievable in Ukraine. That's what we're trying to find out," Rubio said. "I don't think anyone here is claiming that we're on the verge of a negotiated settlement."
Evacuation From Russian-Occupied Oleshky Completed, Kyiv And Moscow Say
He said President Donald Trump's envoys, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, were devoting much of their time to the Ukraine and Iran portfolios. "But I'm not here to tell you we're on the verge of one," Rubio said, adding that he hoped an agreement could eventually be reached.
He also clarified that Ukraine negotiations were not discussed at the Atlanta G20 gathering itself.
Rubio was equally careful when asked whether Putin would attend the December summit, which Trump plans to host at his Doral resort in Florida.
"I don't even know if President Putin is going to come to Miami. They haven't announced that and they haven't confirmed that," he said.
The three European officials told RFE/RL that Rubio had privately expressed doubts the Russian leader would accept the invitation.
They also said the secretary of state defended the administration's decision to invite Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov to Atlanta and extend an invitation to Putin, arguing that diplomatic engagement was necessary to achieve a settlement.
"How can you have a negotiated settlement between Russia and Ukraine if you don't have the ability to talk to both Russia and Ukraine?" Rubio later asked when pressed by reporters.
He said Trump did not regard meeting or talking with a foreign leader as legitimizing that leader's actions or agreeing with everything they stood for.
Rubio also cited Russia's nuclear arsenal as a reason for maintaining communication between Washington and Moscow, regardless of the state of bilateral relations.
"It is always important that the United States and Russia have communications at some level because of the danger of escalation in the future," he said.
Describing his own interaction with Lavrov in Atlanta, Rubio said the two had not held a formal meeting. They spoke briefly about the possibility of their countries' leaders interacting at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering, but made no firm commitments concerning the G20 summit.
Marriage Of Convenience: Russia And Iran Deepen Trade Ties, But Their Partnership Has Limits
The Western officials said Rubio's private assessment also covered Ukraine's potential NATO membership, which he reportedly described as unrealistic in the short term and unacceptable to Putin.
Rubio reportedly warned that Russia's acquisition of the entire Donbas region would not satisfy the Kremlin's territorial ambitions. It "will not end Russian appetite," he told the Europeans, according to the officials.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reported private remarks.
While Rubio offered little public optimism about a comprehensive peace agreement, he identified a more limited diplomatic objective that Washington hopes could produce results: a cease-fire covering the Black Sea.
European officials pressed Moscow during the Atlanta talks to halt attacks affecting shipping in the strategic waterway, which is vital for Ukrainian agricultural exports.
Putin Has Shown No Willingness To End Ukraine War, Says Mike Pompeo
Rubio warned that disruptions to grain and energy shipments were creating serious consequences for vulnerable countries, particularly those dependent on food imports. "This is threatening the world for food security and some energy security as well," he said.
The issue was also raised by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul on October 31. Zelenskyy thanked Ankara for supporting Ukraine's sovereignty and efforts to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
The Atlanta gathering exposed deep divisions between Moscow and European governments, with Lavrov's presence prompting several delegations to refuse participation in the traditional G20 family photograph. The photograph was ultimately canceled.
As Lavrov Returns To G20, Ukraine, Middle East Highlight Western Divisions

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Lavrov of presenting false narratives about the war during the discussions.
Kallas told reporters that Russia did not appear ready for peace negotiations, pointing to the continued intensity of attacks on Ukraine.
Lavrov, meanwhile, criticized what he called Europe's "arrogant boycott" and praised the Trump administration's willingness to engage with Moscow.
Rubio said the US remained committed to exploring a diplomatic solution, describing the war as devastating for both countries.
He pointed to Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and rising civilian casualties, while also citing the heavy Russian military losses. He estimated that around 20,000 Russians were being killed each month.
"It's a very deadly and destructive war," Rubio said, warning that every additional month of fighting would make the eventual reconstruction of Ukraine more difficult.
He described Washington's central objective as determining whether it could use its contacts with both sides to facilitate an end to the conflict.
The two-day ministerial ended without a joint communique, as disagreements over Ukraine, the Middle East, trade, and maritime security prevented the world's largest economies from reaching consensus.

Alex Raufoglu is RFE/RL's senior correspondent in Washington, D.C.

items.title: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
items.summary: French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween, as some 320,000 people nationwide took to the streets.
items.content:
Europe roiled by more youth-led protests French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween, as some 320,000 people nationwide took to the streets.
France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
A demonstrator holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday.
PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.
Is this how the great international borrowing spree ends?
France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.
Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.
At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.
The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.
Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.
Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."
The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.
What Do The Protests Across Europe Mean For The Continent?
Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.
Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.
The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.
While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.
Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.
Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands
In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.
Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.
Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.
Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.
In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

Young Iranians walk past a large anti-US wall mural in Tehran on Sunday. Iran’s foreign minister has said he hopes the US chooses ‘diplomacy over other paths’ to end the crisis. Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images
Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”
Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.
In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the country was ready for both defence and diplomacy. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution. Photograph: Erik S Lesser/AFP/Getty Images Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.
Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”
Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe Close
Hundreds of thousands of protesters demonstrated across France as the country prepares for a general strike in the coming days.
In Paris, police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in a third weekend of nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services.
More than 320,000 people took to the streets around the country and at least 290 protesters were arrested, according to France's interior ministry. Police say about 70,000 demonstrated in Paris.
The authorities prepared extensively to avoid a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that happened two weeks ago.
Protests also took place in Albania, Germany and Italy as youth take to the streets across Europe, the BBC's correspondent James Waterhouse reports.

items.title: US, Israeli targets, timelines, priorities for a potential third Iran war - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: US, Israeli targets, timelines, priorities for a potential third Iran war  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Israel, US have plan ready for third Iran war, Tehran's hidden weapons pose challenges - analysis
Israeli officials have pressed Trump to deal with Pickaxe Mountain, and anytime he has made threats relating to the facility, Iran has made clear ot views it as a top strategic asset.
SATELLITE VIEW shows vehicles at an entrance to Pickaxe Mountain tunnels, near Natanz nuclear facility, in Iran, June 21.
How a third Iran war would be fought has already taken shape.
Foreign sources have reported that the Israeli Air Force flew through Syria and Iraq up to the Iranian border to rehearse its strikes on the Islamic Republic.
Israel has already used its F-35s to outwit and eliminate Iran's radar four times dating back to April 2024, followed by using its F-15s and F-16s to carry out massive bombing raids.
Over 200 Israeli fighter jets struck the Islamic Republic in the first wave in February of this year.
The US and Israel carved up Iran into sectors, with Israel focused on the western and Tehran sectors, and American forces focused on the southern sector and some targets in the Tehran region.
Allied air power in formation: Israel Air Force F-16 fighter jets fly in formation during a mission against Iran, as the US and Israel conduct unprecedented, fully integrated multi-domain operations against Iranian military targets. (credit: IDF Spokesperson’s Office)
This plan worked and is likely to repeat itself on some level, with the first goal being to establish air supremacy so that drones, which are easier to shoot down than fighter jets but have advantages in being able to stand over a target for an extensive time period, can take a large role in the battle.
There is little Iran can do to prevent Israeli and US aircraft dominance.
Pickaxe Mountain: The facility where Iran could secretly make nuclear weapons
US President Donald Trump has focused the most on the Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.
The reason is not that the facility is already operational, as sources have conveyed to The Jerusalem Post that it still is not.
Rather, the reason is that it is unclear whether either Israeli or even US aircraft using mega 30,000 bunker-buster bombs can destroy it.
And if Iran succeeded in moving both highly enriched uranium and centrifuges to that facility, as well as making it operational, it could conceivably sneak out to a nuclear weapon without anyone knowing or being able to do anything about it from the air.
The US used 12 of its 30,000-pound Massive Ordnance Penetrator (MOP) bombs to destroy Iran's Fordow nuclear facility.
Fordow was deep enough under a mountain that many senior Israeli military officials believed it could not be damaged long-term by the smaller Israeli weapons.
The nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain is much deeper underground, such that more defense experts have raised doubts that even the US MOP bombs can destroy it.
In that case, the best moves would be to cause cave-ins across the facility before any important nuclear material, machinery, or know-how makes it into the facility.
Israeli officials have pressed Trump to deal with it, and anytime he has made threats relating to the facility, Iran has responded with harsh language, showing it also views the facility as one of its top strategic assets.
Think tank identifies potential weak points at Pickaxe Mountain
A new survey of the facility published on Friday by the Institute for Science and International Security focuses on two ventilation shafts as possible targets to better strike the insides of the facility: the probable ventilation port/shaft north of the ridge and the possible ventilation shaft south of the ridge.
This think tank report also flags the eastern and western primary tunnel entrances as the main likely points from which the Iranians would likely try to transport nuclear assets into the facility under the mountain.
All of these locations would need to be struck at a minimum to try to disrupt the facility's functioning, but it is a large, sprawling facility with many other assets noticeable from satellite footage, which would also likely need to be struck.
Of course, that is still only one strategic target.
How will Israel handle Iran's underground ballistic missile facilities?
In early 2026, Israel and the US mostly caused cave-ins at these facilities, only to find that within days and sometimes less than a day, Iran's bulldozer crews were able to reopen areas which had been caved in.
Even over the nearly 40-day war, Israeli tactics did not change much and did little to solve this issue.
In addition, between the June 2025 and early 2026 wars, Iran altered its ballistic missile strategy.
Instead of trying to fire concentrated huge barrages from a small number of centralized locations, it spread out its missile crews across the country, and often fired only small barrages at a time.
While these small barrages did not threaten massive nationwide harm, they did cause much of the country to regularly shut down, as they were more frequent and continuous.
Also, Iran watched where Israel was centering its air defense, and adapted mid-war to strike other areas, at one point striking Israel's South with a high degree of lethality only days after the IDF had said the South could go back to its more regular routine for lack of Iranian missiles being fired at it.
In early 2026, Iran also managed to destroy American bases in several countries, causing at least $5 billion in damage.
All of this means that Iran can yield air supremacy to Israel and the US, while still managing to wreak havoc across the region, including against Israel.
Has Israel figured out new techniques to take out the underground missile cities for longer, to find and destroy spread out missile crews, and to prevent Iran from taking advantage of Israel's shortage in air defense systems and interceptors?
Will the operation last a few days or run on for weeks?
Trump has said he wants a fast and "clean" three-day operation, but Iran's regime does not need to cooperate.
They have said they will fire more directly on US ships, on underwater internet cables, and on critical energy facilities of US allies.
Already, the Saudis have faced mass-casualty lethal attacks from the Houthis on high profile economic and transport facilities.
If Iran retains ballistic missiles, some of its nuclear assets which remain under rubble, drones, and the ability to harass naval ships trying to pass through Hormuz, will it change its fundamental negotiating position because its military damage went from $200-300 billion to $220-320 billion?
Many Israelis are skeptical that anything but a longer and more sustained operation will change Iran's behavior.
Likewise, some Israelis, such as former defense minister Yoav Gallant, have suggested that only a ground operation, not airstrikes, can neutralize some of Iran's highly enriched uranium buried deep underground.
Will Israel and the US finally strike Iran's top energy facilities, which some Mossad officials believed could lead to regime change at an earlier date?
Or will they hold back fearing such strikes will turn Iranians into supporting their regime and against any outsiders?
What will happen when Trump wants to end the conflict earlier than Israel, and given that he, and especially his advisors, have lost interest or faith in any near-term regime change?
How will Israelis feel about having been shot at by Iranian ballistic missiles for the fifth time in three years without the latest operation seeming to lead to a clearer end game regarding at least the nuclear threat, let alone the ballistic missile threat, or leading to regime change?
There is no question that a US and Israeli third war against Iran can push off the nuclear, and especially the ballistic missile threats deeper into the future.
But it is unclear how Israel will grade the success of such an operation.

items.title: Iran to receive Russian Su-35 fighter jets after US-Iran war ends, IRGC spokesman says - report - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: Iran to receive Russian Su-35 fighter jets after US-Iran war ends, IRGC spokesman says - report  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Iran to receive Russian Su-35 fighter jets after US-Iran war ends, IRGC spokesman says - report
While the IRGC spokesperson did not specifically name Russia in the interview, it is the only established manufacturer of Su-35s.
Russian Sukhoi Su-35 jet fighters fire missiles during the Aviadarts competition, as part of the International Army Games 2021, at the Dubrovichi range outside Ryazan, Russia August 27, 2021.
Iran will reportedly receive Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets after the US-Iran war ends, Revolutionary Guards spokesman General Mohammad Akraminia told Iranian media on Sunday.
Akraminia claimed that before the war began at the end of February, the IRGC was in the final stages of procuring the fighter jets. He told the Persian-language outlet Tabnak that the Su-35s were meant to arrive before the war.
Akramina did not elaborate as to why they were not delivered before the fighting began.
“We had already completed the necessary preliminary work, including the procurement process and the signing of contracts. The necessary work concerning pilot training and instruction had also been completed, and there were no longer any problems in that regard,” he said.
“In fact, these aircraft were supposed to arrive before the war. God willing, we will certainly receive them after the war and upgrade our air fleet.”
Smoke rises following an explosion in Tehran amid the war with Iran, March 7, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. (credit: MAJID ASGARIPOUR/WANA (WEST ASIA NEWS AGENCY) VIA REUTERS)
Iran claims it plans to strengthen air defenses after war with US
Akraminia added that the IRGC plans to roll out more advanced aircraft, including the Su-35.
“We have also made progress domestically. Of course, purchasing equipment from abroad will bring us closer to advanced technologies, which we can then use as a foundation for further development,” he added.
While he did not specifically name Russia in the interview, it is the only established manufacturer of Su-35s. The fighter jet is Russian-designed and produced by Sukhoi, part of Russia's United Aircraft Corporation.
However, Russia allows other countries, including Iran, to operate the fighter jets.
Akraminia added that Iran is working to develop ground-based and airborne radar systems, as well as satellites to strengthen the country’s air defenses.
“When you operate an advanced aircraft such as the Su-35, you must also have ground-based systems, airborne systems, and satellite capabilities supporting it. Only then can the aircraft reach its full operational potential,” he added.
Akraminia noted that the US sanctions against Iran have made it difficult to rebuild the country’s military.
“Sometimes sanctions affect trade, goods, oil, and similar areas. But they also affect defense and military technologies,” he said.
“The Americans have absolutely refused to allow these new technologies to enter our country. They have imposed very severe sanctions.
“Everything we have achieved, all  the capabilities you mentioned, has been developed domestically through the efforts of our own specialists and young people working in the country's defense industries, universities, and knowledge-based companies.”
He then claimed that during both wars with the US, Iran “did not use a single foreign-produced weapon.”

items.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
items.summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
items.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.
The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said , external the US is still unsure who the culprits are.
"We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.
From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.
Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.
The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

items.title: Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war - Al Jazeera
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.?oc=5" target=
items.content:
Share Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war on social media
Iran’s Foreign Minister speaks to Al Jazeera about US proposals
Tehran, Iran – Ongoing contacts through mediators have provided a potential diplomatic opening between Iran and the United States, even as both sides express readiness for renewed military escalation.
After two days of Qatari-mediated talks, Iranian authorities have signalled that a deal remains possible provided that their demands are tangibly implemented. At the same time, they have doubled down on a willingness to expand attacks or even launch preemptive strikes if they deem war is inevitable.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”
His comments came as US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the talks were going “fine” but added that Iranian authorities were not “reliable”.
The Republican leader, who ordered attacks alongside Israel against Iran on February 28, has repeatedly raised prospects of once more hitting the country’s civilian infrastructure. In recent weeks, he has suggested that an attack could potentially take place after the November 3 midterm elections in the US.
“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida about further bombing Iran’s nuclear facilities.
The mediated talks in Tehran on Friday, and then in Qatar on Saturday, appear to have produced a new tangible result by shortening the period after which Iran’s proposal to partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz can be enforced.
Tehran had previously offered seven days, but that has now come down to two, Araghchi said in his interview with Al Jazeera.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said there are “indications” of US interest in a negotiated settlement, citing the continuing Qatar-mediated talks and US Vice President JD Vance’s recent outreach .
“However, Iran is seeking a series of concessions while the United States insists on progress on Iran’s nuclear programme before concessions are made,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore the central difficulty is sequencing and leverage. Each side wants the other to act first.”
Araghchi’s two-day offer indicates some flexibility over sequencing that could also allow both sides to claim an initial diplomatic achievement without immediately resolving their fundamental disagreements, according to Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.
“However, the military statements show the limits of this opening. Iran appears increasingly determined to prevent a repetition of previous scenarios in which negotiations or temporary ceasefires were followed by renewed military conflict,” he wrote on social media. “From Tehran’s perspective, the objective is to make another attack so costly and unpredictable that Washington would have to reconsider the option altogether.”
As the talks were ongoing on Saturday, the office of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he had a meeting earlier with top military commanders to demand “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for an immediate response “without geographical restriction” to any threat.
Targets would include “tangible and intangible” US and Israeli assets, Khamenei said. Iranian authorities have previously said if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is attacked again, seabed cables and infrastructure across the region could also become targets.
After Khamenei’s statement, commanders of the general staff of the armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the traditional army separately expressed readiness to launch missile, drone and other attacks in case of an escalation of conflict.
State media on Sunday also aired footage of missiles and drones being taken out of massive underground storage sites and deployed during the eight months of war so far.
The authorities also signalled that they expect more potential attacks from the US and Israel, including against Iran’s power grid.
Gholamreza Jalali, commander of the National Organization for Passive Defense, said during a speech on Sunday that they have identified 14 sectors most dependent on electricity that would need support if the war restarts, without naming any.
“Adopting preventive measures in the area of passive defence for the electricity grid is a fundamental principle that all authorities must follow up in their capacities,” he said, adding that officials were considering “network islanding” practices to create different segments that would not all be simultaneously affected by potential bombing.
In and around the Strait of Hormuz, vessels continue to be attacked if they refuse to coordinate with the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the entity set up by Iranian authorities to enforce control and sovereignty in the critical waterway.
At least four tankers were identified as being hit on Friday and Saturday, although not all attacks are reported by vessels and monitors. According to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a vessel carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) was struck by three Iranian projectiles on Saturday about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran’s Lavan Island, deep into the Gulf.
Transit in the strait and surrounding waterways will not return to normal unless the US takes steps towards Iran’s conditions, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told state television during an interview on Saturday night.
For the sequencing to work, he said Tehran wants the US to lift its naval blockade that has halted oil exports and the majority of Iran’s trade, which used to be facilitated through its southern ports. The US must also issue waivers for oil sanctions, unfreeze Iran’s assets abroad, stop fighting on all regional fronts, including Lebanon, and recognise a bilateral Iran-Oman arrangement for Hormuz.
Rezaei said he has yet to respond to a letter addressed to him by Vance, although he said the missive indicated a “change in tone” that he described as “positive”.
Mostafa Najafi, a Tehran-based political analyst said to be linked with Rezaei, said if the conditions are not met, the letter is likely to go unanswered and negotiations – including on Iran’s nuclear programme – will not enter a higher level.
“It is unclear how willing Washington is to accept these demands. It is clear that not recognising rights emphasised by Iran will lead to the failure of the negotiations,” he wrote on X.
The US has also doubled down on the effectiveness of its Operation Economic Outcast involving the blockade, sanctions and pressure on overland trade and aviation.
A report by the US Treasury to inform Trump’s decision-making, which was publicised by news outlet Axios, said no new oil had been loaded onto tankers at Iran’s terminals since August 25. It also showed overseas crude deliveries were down, while Iran’s year-on-year inflation neared 90 percent in September and the national currency continued to dwindle.
The report said Iran’s economy was “crippled” by the combined measures, but did not argue that it was close to collapsing.

Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.
Dr Marta Shahbazi , an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.
The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.
In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Martha was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”
It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.
Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.
“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her. Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did …
“My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”
The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela, Spain , paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.
The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.
Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” and has promised an investigation .

items.content:
A riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France. Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images
A riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France. Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images
Attempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot police
Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania
French officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.
In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces in Switzerland were attacked with paving stones.
Protests over the education system, deteriorating public services, declining prospects, unaffordable housing and the spiralling cost of living have shaken a number of countries this autumn.
Violence erupted in the French capital as well as Marseille, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Lyon and Toulouse on Saturday night after an estimated 320,000 demonstrators, some in Halloween costumes, took to the streets.
Protesters in Halloween costumes gather in the La Plaine square in Marseille. Officials say 320,000 people took part in protests across France. Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty Images View image in fullscreen
Protesters in Halloween costumes at an unauthorised demonstration in Marseille over the high cost of living. Photograph: Coust Laurent/ABACA/Shutterstock As the rallies ended, masked and hooded rioters arrived and caused what the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as an “extraordinary” level of violence. More than 770 people were arrested.
In Paris, the prosecutor’s office said incendiary devices were thrown at a group of about 15 gendarmes and police officers and a formal investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Injuries reportedly included second-degree burns in an incident captured on mobile phone video and shared on social media and broadcast on French television.
The level of physical violence and looting was significantly lower than on 17 October, when 2,600 people were arrested and as many as 3,000 shops pillaged in one of the worst nights of urban unrest in France’s recent history.
Riot police in action in Paris. More than 770 people were arrested across France for public order offences. Photograph: Bernard Jules/ABACA/Shutterstock In Germany, looters and rioters ⁠rampaged through Frankfurt, the country’s financial hub, damaging stores and injuring more than 100 police officers.
“The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,” said Alexander Dobrindt, the hardline interior minister. He singled out “violent leftwing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community”, adding: “Tough penalties must follow this breach of the peace.”
Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that deploying a heavy police presence across multiple locations had been effective. “Excesses of ​violence like those ‌in Paris were ​prevented thanks to our ​highly committed police forces,” he said.
A protester in a Batman costume salutes in front of a fire started by rioters in Frankfurt. German authorities have promised a strong response. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters More than 100,000 protesters marched in over 30 German cities on Saturday to demand better ⁠education and lower living costs in protests led by the “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z will sort it) campaign.
Hooded rioters ⁠damaged 17 Frankfurt shops, looting five of them, and threw missiles including petrol bombs, according to Roman Poseck, the state interior minister for Hesse.
More than 100 of the 1,300 police officers deployed in the city were injured and 54 suspects, ‌aged from 13 to 29, were arrested. “I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.
Most of those arrested were German nationals, the minister said, adding that police estimated they had been confronted with “between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background”.
Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked police with bottles and fireworks. Gen Z regelt posted a statement distancing itself from all violence.
Riot police clear Lisbon’s Rossio Square of activists protesting over housing affordability. Photograph: Manuel de Almeida/EPA In Portugal , riot police removed protesters by force from Rossio Square in Lisbon at about 4.30am on Sunday after thousands of people angry at the housing crisis marched through the city on Saturday and set up camp.
The protesters want Portugal’s minority centre-right government to withdraw a ⁠bill that makes ⁠evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases. A smaller camp in Porto was also cleared by force.
In Albania , masked protesters hurled stones and firebombs at police in the capital, Tirana, on the margins of a demonstration demanding the resignation of the prime minister, Edi Rama, over perceived corruption.
Youths threw paving stones and firebombs at police and set fire to rubbish bins at the end of a largely peaceful protest. The interior ministry said on Friday that 350 people had been hurt in the protests, including 200 police, with 269 minors arrested.
An anti-government protest in Tirana turned violent with protesters hurling stones and petrol bombs at police. Photograph: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/Shutterstock In Switzerland, hundreds of protesters gathered in Zürich and Basel on Saturday night for unauthorised demonstrations – both of which ended in violence – under the slogan: “We’ve had enough in Switzerland, too.”
In Zürich, police used water cannon, teargas and rubber bullets to disperse rioters attacking them with fireworks, bottles and stones, Swiss media reported . A police patrol car was damaged and rubbish bins and electric bikes set on fire.
In Basel, police said about 150 people gathered in the city centre at around 9pm. Shop windows were smashed, facades tagged with graffiti and bins and bikes set on fire, with incidents also reported in Geneva.

items.title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
items.summary: The protests in cities across Germany - including Berlin, Hamburg and Frankfurt - came on the same day hundreds of thousands also protested in France.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in Germany
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.
Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.
Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."
Image caption, Police detain a demonstrator dressed as Batman in Frankfurt
Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.
The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
"We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Image caption, People try to break through a window of a Frankfurt shop selling weapons
Similar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind".
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
Figure caption, Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.
Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off , but French newspaper Le Monde has reported , external that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.
