items.title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - could Talarico turn the tide?
items.summary: The state's $500m Senate race may be the most closely watched in the US midterms, and is about far more than control of Congress.
items.content:
Image caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate races
The race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year â a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.
For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.
But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988.
That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans.
"If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.
These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.
For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat.
At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.
In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual.
"It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."
When Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters â with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.
He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate.
"Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."
The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning â "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" â is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.
His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music. He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.
In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state.
"A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."
Image caption, Donald Trump won Texas in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential elections
For Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.
At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump â alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton â was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size.
"If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.
Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans.
"Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."
Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X.
"When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."
For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.
They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia.
"I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser.
"The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."
Image caption, Republican candidate Ken Paxton has a Trump endorsement - and some past controversies in Texas politics
For the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics â a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser.
"Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."
But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.
The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one.
Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.
Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.
Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?
Texas-specific issues have also contributed to a hostile climate for the in-power party.
Polling and recent special elections in Texas indicate that Hispanic voters â many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 â have soured on the administration's immigration enforcement policies.
Hispanics make up nearly a third of the state's population - and in more than a week of early voting in Texas, they have been casting ballots in historically large numbers.
Data centre construction, which Texas Republicans had touted as a welcome investment in the state, has drawn widespread criticism, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally been solidly conservative.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott, in his own tight re-election race, recently announced a one-year moratorium on AI construction in the state â a reflection of how quickly the issue has become a political liability.
"It's bad for Republicans," one Texas political strategist, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC. "We're asking a whole lot of the electorate at this point for us to continue to be the guys in charge."
Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms
Then there's the baggage that Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a contentious primary campaign earlier this year, brings to the race.
The 63-year-old Republican successfully painted the 74-year-old Cornyn as too old and too out-of-touch with Texas conservatives. He received a late boost, just days before his run-off election victory over Cornyn, in the form of a Trump endorsement.
"Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness."
The "a lot" the president referenced Paxton going through includes a 2015 federal indictment on charges of securities fraud â later dropped â and a 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives on corruption, bribery and abuse of power charges.
The Texas Senate would later acquit Paxton after Trump intervened to pressure state Republican leaders.
All of this has meant that Paxton has more than a few critics â and enemies - in Texas, including within his own party.
EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midterms
IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope
Talarico, by contrast, has proven to be an effective candidate. The state legislator defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary.
Since earning the nomination, he has maintained his polling lead despite a withering onslaught of negative advertising - much of it funded by the world's richest man Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in Texas.
Musk alone has funnelled more than $170m into the race . Trump's MAGA Inc. committee has chipped in $40m.
While Paxton has proven to be an ineffective fundraiser, the third-party money spent on his behalf has blanketed the airwaves in the state â spilling over into sporting events involving Texas teams that air across the nation.
They have targeted Talarico for his past comments supporting transgender people, for calling "radicalised white men" a domestic terrorism threat and for criticising the fossil fuel and beef industries â two powerful interests in the state.
Talarico has distanced himself from some of those earlier comments, arguing many were taken out of context and "missed the mark" or were "deliberately provocative" or "cringy".
Meanwhile, the Texas Democrat has proven to be a historically successful fundraiser, amassing more than $140m in donations over the course of his campaign and setting a three-month fundraising record for a Senate candidate.
The funding has allowed Talarico to hit back at Paxton, highlighting his past controversies, and defending himself from Republican attacks.
He frequently leans into his religious upbringing â as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary â leavening his stump speeches with biblical references.
There is one particular passage Talarico has been partial to of late â the familiar Old Testament showdown between scrappy David and the giant Goliath.
"We are going up against our own Goliaths," he said in Lubbock. "The billionaire mega-donors, the corporate special interests, the entire Washington DC establishment. Their power is real, but so is ours."
But the power of Texas Democrats has been overestimated in the past. In 2018, Congressman Beto O'Rourke posted his own historic fundraising numbers, generated serious national attention and ultimately lost to Texas Senator Cruz by just over 2%.
Talarico's polling lead, while stable, continues to rest near the margin of error in most surveys. And last-minute Republican appeals, as well as Trump's repeated campaign visits, could spur conservatives to turn out in greater numbers on election day, erasing any Democratic early voting advantages.
Inside the tiny Democratic Party office at a Talarico rally in Amarillo on Tuesday, retired schoolteacher Terri Mills listened to the candidate's stump speech.
Despite acknowledging the decades of Democratic futility and false dawns, she said she was allowing herself to hope for a Democratic victory once again.
"I have gotten my hopes up before, you know," she said. "But I do feel that this time is a little different."

Giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically. Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News
Giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically. Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News
UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme
Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.
The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.
British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.
Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on Brexit
On Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reeves praised the prime minister , Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.
Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.
But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.
One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”
Andy Burnham with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, in September. Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”
Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and to lay out options for how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry.
In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.
Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota.
The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.
What makes Andy Burnham think we can rejoin the EU? | Politics Weekly
British access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles.
EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiations to a standstill this year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.
The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.
EU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.
Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. France dropped its opposition to the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.
Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely, deferring any agreement for six months . But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.
Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.
Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.
Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.
UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.
The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme, prompting warnings from the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.
This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, recently told the Guardian he would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.
The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.
The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.

items.title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading - The Guardian
items.summary: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading  The Guardian
items.content:
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Donald Trump ’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.
The port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires
The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.
Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.
By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.
China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.
A girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026. Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/Reuters It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions . While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.
Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.
China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions , covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.
One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.
Workers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China. Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty Images China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.
This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?
The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

items.title: University of Cambridge scientist among those who died in Spanish train crash
items.summary: Marta Shahbazi was an "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist", says the laboratory where she worked.
items.content:
Image caption, Dr Marta Shahbazi, pictured in 2024, was travelling to collect a prize at an awards ceremony in her native Spain when she died
An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.
The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.
The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.
"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Image caption, Shahbazi joined the Cambridge laboratory in 2020
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.
"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post , external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.
The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.

Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, with a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky due to end late on Sunday.
Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.
The Wall Street Journal had reported that Ukraine had given in to pressure from the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper that they never agreed to a demand from Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.
Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.
Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s ongoing “long-range sanctions”.
A satellite image shows smoke rising from the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region on Russia after a reported Ukrainian drone attack on Friday. Photograph: European Union/Copernicus/Sentinel-2/Reuters Zelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the ​deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram. Kyiv experienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.
Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sqkm (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sqkm (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”
The latest attacks came as a six-day local ceasefire brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, was due to come to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residents were reunited with their loved ones over the weekend in northern Ukraine , with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.
Ukrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleskhy. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.
The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between ⁠Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would ⁠pave the ⁠way ​for broader peace efforts.
“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.
Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, with Kremlin officials saying on Sunday that Vladimir Putin was willing to talk directly with Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.
There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged. He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces which the Kremlin does not control, but says it has “annexed”.

Shell Receives First Commercial LNG Cargo From US’ Venture Global
British energy giant Shell has received the first liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo under a long-term sales contract from US-based Venture Global’s Plaquemines export facility in Louisiana, following the start of commercial operations at the plant’s first phase, Venture Global said on press release published on November 1.
The Malaga Knutsen LNG tanker loaded the cargo and departed on October 31, marking the start of deliveries under long-term contracts at Plaquemines Phase 1, the company added.
“Achieving commercial operations at the first phase of our second LNG project in 53 months is a testament to our team’s relentless dedication and hard work,” Venture Global’s CEO Mike Sabel said.
“We are thrilled to hit another major milestone that enables us to continue delivering reliable, affordable American LNG to the global market. We deeply appreciate the collaboration of our regulators and supply chain partners, whose shared commitment helped us deliver this project safely and on schedule,” Sabel added.
The first phase completed commissioning about 22 months after producing its first LNG. Other long-term customers expected to receive volumes include Poland’s Orlen, China’s Sinopec, CNOOC Gas & Power and France’s EDF, according to Reuters .
Contract prices are expected to be significantly below recent highs of around $34 per million British thermal units (mmbtu) at Europe’s Dutch Title Transfer Facility benchmark and $32/mmbtu at Asia’s Japan-Korea Marker, Reuters reported.
Shell is a major global LNG trader and buyer, purchasing volumes from multiple suppliers to serve customers worldwide. Its integrated gas business spans LNG production, trading, shipping and marketing.

items.summary: These 3 AI Stocks Could Soon Enter the S&P 500. Are They Worth Buying Before the Move?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is creating opportunities beyond tech giants. Astera Labs ( ALAB -10.93% ) , Credo Technology Group ( CRDO -8.65% ) , and Sanmina ( SANM -4.33% ) are three promising companies benefiting from rising AI spending . None of the three was added to the S&P 500 in September, and the next rebalance should take effect Dec. 21.
To be included in the S&P 500, a company requires a market capitalization of at least $22.7 billion and positive earnings. If AI spending continues to drive massive growth, these stocks could emerge as future S&P 500 candidates, potentially rewarding investors who get in early.
Astera Labs, the largest of the three by market value, comes first.
1. Connectivity chips are driving Astera Labs' rapid growth
Astera Labs develops connectivity solutions that move data between chips, memory, and other components in AI systems. As these systems become more complex, the connections between them can become a bottleneck. Astera's products are addressing that challenge. The company is already expanding beyond its established connectivity products.

Its Scorpio fabric switches help connect large numbers of AI chips, while its optical connectivity and custom solutions offer greater opportunities as AI data centers evolve.
With Astera, investors demand solid growth, as evidenced by the stock's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of almost 45 times. But the results are already showing up in earnings.
Astera has also attracted attention as a potential S&P 500 addition; in fact, its $45 billion market cap already clears S&P's $22.7 billion minimum. The main risk, however, is that its growth depends heavily on AI spending, while competition and changing connectivity standards could challenge its position.
Meanwhile, another company is tackling the broader challenge of moving data across advanced AI data centers.
2. Optical products could widen Credo's reach in AI data centers
Credo develops high-speed connectivity products spanning copper and optical solutions, helping customers move data reliably across AI infrastructure . Its portfolio includes active electrical cables, optical digital signal processors, and other networking products.
One of the most interesting developments is Credo's expansion into optical connectivity. Although copper is useful for short-distance connections, optical technology can become more attractive as data rates and transmission distances grow. This gives the company broad exposure to various networking hardware used in AI data centers.

Its combination of growth, profitability, and expanding product opportunities makes Credo a possible S&P 500 candidate. At $33 billion, its market value already tops S&P's $22.7 billion minimum. It was also identified among possible additions in September 2026.
That said, the company faces risks around customer concentration, competition, and reliance on AI spending. And with the stock trading at 28 times forward P/E, it could look reasonable to investors backing its AI-driven growth.
The next company offers a unique way to invest in the AI boom by manufacturing hardware that keeps data centers running.
3. Manufacturing hardware gives Sanmina a role in AI data centers
Sanmina provides manufacturing solutions for electronic and industrial systems. Its work spans areas like communications networks and cloud infrastructure. As data center operators expand their infrastructure, the demand for reliable manufacturing partners will only accelerate.
Building out data centers requires more than just chips; it involves networking equipment, power systems, and other hardware. And Sanmina's manufacturing capabilities allow it to participate in that broader supply chain.
To further strengthen its capabilities, it acquired ZT Systems' manufacturing business to expand its presence in cloud and AI infrastructure manufacturing.

The risk is that the company earns lower margins than many chip designers, while customer concentration and slower data center spending could affect growth. But at a forward P/E ratio of just over 12, the stock could be a more value-oriented way to invest in the AI boom.
The question now is whether these three companies can sustain their growth and meet the requirements for inclusion in the S&P 500.
These AI stocks could be the S&P 500's next additions
Astera Labs, Credo Technology, and Sanmina are well-positioned to benefit from the AI spending boom, and continued growth could bring them closer to joining the S&P 500.
Investors willing to get in early may want to keep these three stocks on their radar. If these companies continue to expand, an S&P 500 inclusion announcement could be around the corner, potentially giving their shares a major boost.

How Rachel Reeves has mapped out economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s government
On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her
Which senior politician has argued that “Brexit did deep damage” and that the government seeks “not to turn back the clock but to look toward a new and stable, future relationship?”
It was not Andy Burnham, who has been the torchbearer for thinking the unthinkable on Brexit since he became prime minister. Instead, these are the words of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, in a lecture six months ago.
Reeves has taken a more thoughtful approach on how to come to terms with life outside government than some of her fellow former ministers.
A speech at Harvard on Monday will be her first public intervention on her own record and on Britain’s future, wisely left until after John Healey’s first budget .
She will say no one in government could “be in any doubt” about her view on the damage of Brexit – and her belief that one day the UK should return to the EU fold. “Economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe,” Reeves will say.
The speech, which will examine how governments can meet the public’s appetite for radicalism while maintaining credibility with financial markets, will say that pursuing a closer relationship with the EU, even rejoining, may be credible as well as radical.
“Economically, it is the credible choice. Britain’s values, and a serious assessment of the geopolitical scene today, tell us it is the radical choice too,” she will say, giving Burnham “credit for his willingness to face reality head on”.
The Treasury, where the blueprints for the Remain campaign’s “Project Fear” were drawn up, has always been the heart of pro-European sentiment in government and Reeves its biggest champion under Keir Starmer .
Her sentiment seems more aligned though with that of Burnham, who cast her out of government, than with Healey, her successor as chancellor. He has joked about his own age when asked if the UK would rejoin the EU “in his lifetime”, saying it was his job to “try and make the most of Britain’s position now”.
Within Westminster, there are more than whispers from some MPs that they have judged Reeves’s legacy and influence too harshly. Healey’s first outing at the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok saw its economists lavish praise on his predecessor, saying the UK’s deficit reduction plan “stands out” among G7 peers.
It is particularly striking how the themes of Reeves’s lecture have become the agenda for Burnham’s government. In it, she argued: “Today, what most distinguishes Britain from our closest peers is the relative underperformance of our major cities outside London, compared to their European counterparts.”
Reeves, who is the MP for Leeds West and Pudsey, said the north of England had “waited for far too long, for a government that matches warm words with concerted ambition”.
Her call to “liberate our regions from stifling Whitehall orthodoxies” sounds strikingly Burnhamesque. The main policy announced in the speech? A plan to begin giving regional leaders a share of national taxes “which have, for too long, been allocated by central government”.
That work now forms the centrepiece of Healey’s budget. If this government has its own theory of growth – Brexit and devolution – it is awkward at best that it removed the key backer of both under Starmer.
But Reeves’s main theory of growth was investment, in pursuit of which she raised employers’ national insurance.
That is the other reason for Burnham’s government to be grateful to Reeves – and for which she has received no credit. Those tax raises – despite being unpopular – gave a sense of a government willing to make hard choices while taking the risk to borrow for public investment. The fiscal rules were changed to allow for a multi-year commitment to an eventual £100bn in new capital spending.
The cash is now beginning to flow into NHS infrastructure, roads, housing, rail upgrades and energy and industrial investments. Reeves will lay out her theory in her Harvard speech this week that the shift to an investment-led growth model “required sacrifices” that a Starmer-led government failed to get the public to back.
“The challenge is to make the politics and economics, those dual tests of credibility and radicalism, line up,” Reeves will say.
She will not say – although others have – that much of the problem with Starmer’s government was the man himself, rather than the agenda.
Burnham, if he avoids an early election, may start to see some of that investment bear fruit in public and market confidence, both in upgraded public services and in Britain’s appeal as a location for private investment.
There is much that could derail all this – not least further international turmoil – but when Burnham’s government counts its success on public services, Europe, devolution and growth, Reeves will be able to claim some credit.

Stock market forecast: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley predict what's next after tech selloff
AI spending and disappointing earnings trigger October's technology selloff
Goldman Sachs warns AI investment could reach $1.2 tn in 2027
Morgan Stanley forecasts further S&P 500 downside before recovery
JPMorgan sees strong earnings growth but rising financial risks
Citigroup and RBC Capital Markets reduce technology exposure
Strong corporate profits provide an important counterweight
Federal Reserve policy adds pressure to technology valuations
Apple earnings, US midterms and jobs data will test the market
US stocks ended October with their sharpest technology-led selloff in months, as disappointing corporate guidance, rising artificial intelligence investment costs and tighter financial conditions forced Wall Street to reassess the outlook for 2027.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% on October 30, closing at 25,437.00, while the S&P 500 lost 1.82% to 7,580.07.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 1.09% to 51,770.31.
For October, the Nasdaq dropped 5.3%, its worst monthly performance since March 2025, compared with a 0.9% decline for the S&P 500 and a 1.7% gain for the Dow.
Investment banks remain divided over what comes next. Morgan Stanley sees the possibility of another 5-6% decline in the S&P 500 before the correction ends. Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan maintain year-end targets of 8,000, while Citigroup and RBC Capital Markets have adopted more cautious positioning as investors rotate away from expensive technology stocks.
The central concern is no longer whether demand for AI infrastructure exists. It is whether the companies financing that infrastructure can generate sufficient returns to justify their spending.
AI spending and disappointing earnings trigger October's technology selloff
The latest decline followed quarterly results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel, which exposed different weaknesses across the technology sector.
Alphabet suffered its worst weekly performance since 2011 after third-quarter revenue missed expectations and free cash flow turned negative by approximately $9 bn. The company also indicated that investment in AI infrastructure would continue rising in 2027.
Amazon reported adjusted earnings below expectations and negative trailing 12-month free cash flow of $42.4 bn. Its capital expenditure forecast remains approximately $220 bn for 2026, with management expecting significantly higher spending next year.
Intel delivered one of the most dramatic reactions. Shares plunged 28.6% on October 30, their second-largest daily decline in trading data extending back to 1973. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 bn–$16 bn, substantially below Wall Street's estimate of approximately $17.1 bn.
Intel's data center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.3 bn in the third quarter. However, the company faces weakening PC demand, production constraints and continued challenges in its foundry operations.
Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel from Buy to Neutral and reduced his price target from $145 to $100. The bank argued that growing demand for server processors linked to agentic AI is insufficient to offset near-term weakness in PCs and supply constraints.
The selling spread across semiconductor manufacturers. AMD lost nearly 11% on Friday, while Nvidia fell about 4% and Broadcom declined approximately 5%.
These declines reflect a broader change in market expectations: investors are increasingly distinguishing between companies benefiting from AI infrastructure spending and those capable of converting that investment into sustainable profits.
Goldman Sachs warns AI investment could reach $1.2 tn in 2027
Goldman Sachs Research estimates that global AI investment will exceed $1 tn in 2026, including more than $580 bn in the United States. Its latest analysis projects that capital spending by major hyperscalers could reach $1.2 tn in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028.
According to Goldman Sachs, AI-related investment accounts for almost half of the S&P 500's expected earnings-per-share growth in 2026.
This creates a potential vulnerability. Technology companies are spending heavily on data centers, networking equipment, semiconductors and electricity infrastructure before the full financial returns from those investments become visible.
Higher borrowing costs and accelerating depreciation expenses could weaken future profitability even if demand for computing capacity remains strong.
Goldman's analysis suggests that AI investment could shift from supporting S&P 500 earnings growth in 2026 to becoming a marginal drag by 2028.
The implications extend beyond large technology companies. Data center developers, cloud infrastructure providers and businesses financing projects through debt markets face increasing pressure to demonstrate predictable cash flow.
The latest market correction therefore represents a reassessment of capital efficiency across the AI ecosystem, rather than evidence that demand for artificial intelligence has disappeared.
Morgan Stanley forecasts further S&P 500 downside before recovery
Morgan Stanley's chief US equity strategist Mike Wilson believes the market correction is approaching its final stages, but he does not expect a smooth recovery.
In his October 26 assessment, Wilson identified the 7,100–7,200 range as a potential support area for the S&P 500. That would represent a further decline of approximately 5%–6% from the October 30 closing level of 7,580.07.
Wilson also warned that semiconductor stocks could decline another 10%–15% by mid-November as investors reassess AI financing and demand.
Morgan Stanley notes that approximately 60% of Russell 3000 stocks have already fallen more than 20% from their June levels. That suggests much of the market has undergone a substantial correction even while major indexes remained relatively resilient.
Despite the near-term risks, Morgan Stanley retains its 8,000 year-end S&P 500 forecast. Wilson views additional weakness as a possible opportunity to increase exposure to higher-quality companies.
JPMorgan sees strong earnings growth but rising financial risks
J.P. Morgan Asset Management remains constructive on corporate earnings but is considerably more cautious about prospective market returns.
In its fourth-quarter 2026 Global Equity Views, the investment manager forecast approximately 27% growth in US operating profits this year, excluding valuation gains on private technology investments.
Its global outlook anticipates earnings growth approaching 30% in 2026 and approximately 20% in 2027.
However, JPMorgan's equity team has shifted toward a more neutral assessment of market returns.
The reason is the growing difference between corporate earnings growth and the financial risks associated with generating those earnings.
According to JPMorgan, hyperscalers are increasingly accessing debt markets as investment spending exceeds internally generated cash flow.
The firm is particularly concerned about companies operating AI infrastructure with high leverage and limited financial flexibility.
JPMorgan therefore favors diversification and higher-quality businesses rather than indiscriminate exposure to AI-related shares. Its analysis indicates that strong profits can sustain the broader bull market even while individual companies experience substantial valuation declines.
Citigroup and RBC Capital Markets reduce technology exposure
Not every investment bank is waiting for earnings growth to restore confidence.
Citigroup reduced its tactical exposure to US equities on October 13, removing its overweight recommendation and closing a long position in the equal-weighted S&P 500.
The decision reflected concerns about stretched investor positioning, elevated optimism and deteriorating risk-reward conditions.
The move preceded the latest decline and does not necessarily represent a change to Citigroup's previously published 8,100 year-end index target.
RBC Capital Markets also adjusted its sector allocations ahead of the selloff.
On October 14, chief US equity strategist Lori Calvasina downgraded technology from overweight to market weight and upgraded healthcare from market weight to overweight.
The subsequent market performance reinforced the importance of sector selection. Healthcare substantially outperformed the S&P 500 during October, while technology and communication services came under sustained selling pressure.
Energy also attracted investors seeking exposure to companies benefiting from higher oil prices. ExxonMobil and Chevron advanced on Friday following stronger earnings supported by refining margins.
The divergence suggests that investors are reallocating capital within the US equity market rather than withdrawing uniformly from stocks.
Strong corporate profits provide an important counterweight
The latest earnings data indicate that the broader market's fundamentals remain relatively strong.
According to FactSet's October 30 earnings analysis, 60% of S&P 500 companies have reported third-quarter results. Of those companies, 82% exceeded analysts' earnings estimates, compared with a five-year average of 78%.
Blended earnings growth for the quarter stands at 30.2%, while revenue growth is estimated at 13.4%.
There is an important qualification: companies have exceeded earnings estimates by only 1.9% in aggregate, well below the five-year average surprise of 7.5%.
FactSet also places the S&P 500's forward 12-month price-to-earnings ratio at 18.7, below its five-year average of 19.8.
This helps explain why investment banks have not abandoned their positive earnings forecasts. Nevertheless, forward valuations depend on analysts' projections being achieved. If borrowing costs remain elevated or AI investment generates weaker returns, those expectations may require downward revisions.
Federal Reserve policy adds pressure to technology valuations
The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28 in a 10–2 decision.
Chair Kevin Warsh declined to provide a firm commitment regarding the December meeting.
The decision followed economic figures indicating that US GDP expanded at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, while annual PCE inflation reached 3.6% in September.
Stronger economic activity supports corporate revenue, but persistent inflation limits the Federal Reserve's ability to ease financial conditions.
Interest-rate futures suggest approximately a 75% probability of another rate increase in December.
For technology stocks, tighter policy affects valuations through two channels: a higher discount rate reduces the present value of expected future profits, while more expensive financing weakens returns on debt-funded infrastructure projects.
That combination is particularly challenging for companies whose investment plans require several years before generating positive cash flow.
Apple earnings, US midterms and jobs data will test the market
The first week of November offers several immediate catalysts.
Apple's results will be particularly important because the company's shares have held up better than many large technology peers, making its outlook a test of whether investors continue to favor comparatively less capital-intensive technology businesses.
AMD and Super Micro Computer report on Tuesday, November 3, the same day as the US midterm elections.
Qualcomm and Arm Holdings follow on Wednesday, November 4, providing additional information about semiconductor demand and the smartphone market.
The week concludes with the US employment report on Friday, November 6. Economists expect approximately 60,000 new jobs in October, following an increase of 29,000 in September.
A weaker labor market could reduce expectations for another Federal Reserve rate increase. Conversely, unexpectedly strong employment or persistent wage inflation could reinforce concerns that interest rates will remain elevated.
For November, the most important market indicators will be AI capital expenditure guidance, credit spreads, corporate cash flow and the relationship between earnings growth and valuations.
Wall Street's forecasts suggest that the October selloff has not eliminated the possibility of a year-end recovery. The disagreement is over how much further prices may fall before investors become comfortable financing the next stage of the AI expansion.

items.summary: The Nasdaq Just Flashed a Signal Investors Can't Afford to Ignore. History Says the Stock Market Will Do This Next.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -2.86% ) dropped 5.3% in October, recording its worst monthly performance since President Trump's tariffs rocked the index in early 2025. This time, anxiety surrounding the artificial intelligence boom was the driving force behind the drawdown.
Interestingly, monthly declines of at least 5% are relatively common. In fact, including the latest incident, the Nasdaq has suffered 15 such declines over the last decade, averaging more than once per year.
The Nasdaq Composite plunged in October due to concerns about AI spending
The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% in October as investors fretted over the latest financial results from Alphabet and Amazon , while simultaneously trying to wrap their heads around the huge sums of money that technology companies are spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Capital expenditure (capex) spending among the five largest hyperscalers exceeded $400 billion in 2025, and is now forecast to approach $900 billion in 2026, per JPMorgan Chase . That represents an upward revision from $736 billion earlier in the year. Globally, JPMorgan expects AI capex spending to surpass $5.5 trillion by 2030.
Nevertheless, JPMorgan market strategist Dubravko Lakos-Bujas believes Wall Street is too pessimistic about the situation. "The Street appears to be underwriting the AI data center monetization case: Elevated capex today should ultimately translate into higher revenue, stronger margins, and expanding cash flow."
History says the Nasdaq Composite is headed much higher over the next year
Excluding last month, the Nasdaq Composite has suffered a monthly decline of at least 5% on 14 occasions during the last decade. However, the index has typically recovered quickly. The chart below shows the Nasdaq's one-year return following those incidents.
Nasdaq Monthly Loss of 5% or More Nasdaq 12-Month Return
As shown above, over the last decade, the Nasdaq Composite has returned an average of 24% during the 12-month period following monthly declines of at least 5%. In other words, history says the Nasdaq Composite will climb 24% over the next year.
Of course, past performance is never a guarantee of future results, but Wall Street has a curious tendency to overreact to headlines. Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the most recent quarter, and investors panicked about return on their invested capital with respect to AI infrastructure.
However, those quarterly reports represent a single data point in what will ultimately be a much bigger picture. Personally, I don't think the investment thesis for either company has changed. Both are likely to be major winners as the AI boom unfolds, and AI itself is likely to be the most transformative technology in human history.
Short-term volatility notwithstanding, the AI boom is still a great opportunity for patient investors to make money in the stock market. To that end, now is a good time to purchase shares of the Invesco QQQ Trust ( QQQ -3.47% ) .
The Invesco QQQ Trust is an index fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100, a subset of the Nasdaq Composite. Following the last 14 incidents when the Nasdaq Composite dropped at least 5% in a single month, the Nasdaq-100 returned an average of 26% over the next year. That is a compelling reason to buy a few shares today.

items.title: Here are 3 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
items.summary: The market could use a few victories in the days ahead, which will be filled with more earnings, an election, and jobs data.
items.content:
3 big things we're watching in the stock market this week
The busiest week of third-quarter earnings season ended on a sour note. The market could use a few victories in the days ahead, which will be filled with more quarterly reports and updates on the health of the U.S. labor market. Another big variable: the outcome of Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine which party controls the House and Senate for the next two years. There are six Club stocks reporting earnings this week, and the jobs data will also influence expectations for future Federal Reserve policy. 1. Our focus here is stocks, not politics. But the elections across the country cannot be ignored , given the implications for the AI buildout trade if anti-data-center politicians rack up big victories. If the opposite happens, we're likely to get a relief rally. In addition, President Donald Trump has said he's waiting for the midterms to pass before ordering any new military action against Iran. If tensions are ratcheted up, that could spell bad news for oil prices, bond yields and future inflation — all potential headwinds for equities. Now, let's get into what to expect from our portfolio companies and the jobs report. 2. Earnings: Apple will kick things off Monday after the close. This will be John Ternus' first call as CEO, and he's got his work cut out for him. The iPhone 18 Pro, Duo, and new Mac and home-device offerings give him plenty to work with. However, the stakes have been raised after Intel's disastrous guidance for the current quarter was attributed to inflation-induced demand pressure in the PC market. Therefore, it's the outlook Apple management provides at the end of the prepared remarks that will determine the stock reaction. We're seeking answers to two big questions: Is demand for Apple's products holding up better than the overall market thanks to a more affluent customer base? And how are gross margins looking? Apple has already implemented a series of price hikes on some of its hardware offerings due to rising memory costs, but margins can still be squeezed if the full increase wasn't passed through. Management has to balance price hikes against the risk of demand destruction. Given the hardware memory situation, Apple's high-margin Services business becomes all the more important. As a revenue stream entirely separate from memory costs, we're interested in how much it can protect Apple's overall profitability. Revenue: $ 113.4 billion EPS: $1.99 The question for Eaton is less about big-picture demand for its data center products, as results from Alphabet's Google Cloud, Microsoft , and Amazon indicate the AI buildout is very much intact. Rather, it's about how much progress Eaton has made in increasing manufacturing capacity, and if that's led to further margin expansion. Pricing is another tailwind for Eaton, which reports Tuesday morning. We're also interested in hearing about the progress made in integrating Boyd Thermal , which added liquid cooling to Eaton's portfolio of power distribution units, switchgear, transformers, and other electrical equipment. Any updates on the planned divestiture of its mobility unit , which has been a drag on overall growth, are also helpful. Aerospace missed the mark last quarter, though it was up roughly 13% year over year, so we'll be looking for improvement there. Overall, keep in mind that order growth is a key metric beyond reported sales. The reason? Orders reflect current demand, while sales represent past demand that's been fulfilled — and investors are always looking toward the future. Revenue: $8.5 billion EPS: $3.54 DuPont , which specializes in materials used across a ton of end markets, including healthcare, water safety, construction, automotive, and aerospace, also reports Tuesday. Generally, organic sales growth is a key metric to watch. By end market, healthcare, which includes medical packaging, and water are the ones that excite us most over the long term. The Middle East is an important region for DuPont's water business because countries there rely on advanced purification technologies to provide clean drinking water. It has faced some disruption due to the war in Iran (delayed shipments, project timeline shifts), though it's all been manageable, and strength in the industrial water and semiconductor markets has provided an offset. Will that continue to be the case? Another war-related note: the market will be sensitive to how oil and gas inflation is affecting EBITDA margins (the full-year guide includes a 30-basis-point headwind). Lastly, can growth in non-residential construction minimize the impact of sluggish home construction in the U.S.? Revenue: $1.84 billion EPS: $1.87 Qnity Electronics reports Wednesday, and shares of the semiconductor materials supplier are down almost 20% since the company's blowout earnings report in early August . Is the decline warranted, or will it prove to be a massive opportunity? Considering Intel's guidance on the worsening PC slowdown, commentary on current-quarter demand will carry more weight than the September-quarter results. Can possible weakness in consumer electronics be fully offset by strength in AI chip manufacturing? Intel also flagged a shortage of advanced organic substrates that is limiting chip output. We'll be listening for whether those bottlenecks are disrupting customers' production plans and, by extension, orders for Qnity's materials. Any early commentary on 2027 will be notable, as investors consider the potential for upside amid the AI buildout. Revenue: $1.49 billion EPS: $1.20 This is a market interested in defensive names, and Cardinal Health , which reports Thursday morning, fits the bill. But with shares less than 2% from their all-time highs, there's little room for error. Investors have come to love Cardinal for its ability to deliver double-digit earnings growth, so exceeding EPS estimates is the place to start. On Oct. 1 , Cardinal said it renewed its distribution deal with CVS Health through 2032. Expect analysts to seek color on the economics of that agreement, which lifted an overhang on shares. Other topics to watch for: How are shipments of generic medicines trending? This is a key profit driver for Cardinal, reported within its Pharmaceutical and Specialty Solutions segment. We'll also look for updates on the performance of higher-margin growth areas such as nuclear pharmaceuticals, direct-to-home delivery, and its OptiFreight healthcare logistics platform. These businesses are reported within Cardinal's Other segment. Finally, the impact of high oil prices on its Global Medical Products and Distribution segment — which delivers medical, surgical, and laboratory products to hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers — is worth monitoring. Revenue: $66.6 billion EPS: $2.94 Kimberly-Clark joins Cardinal before the bell Thursday, though the maker of Huggies and Scotts toilet paper already preannounced better-than-feared results on Oct. 15, taking away some of the intrigue. The release of preliminary financial results was likely tied to Kimberly-Clark's efforts to close its blockbuster acquisition of Tylenol maker Kenvue , which is supposed to close by year-end. Could we hear something this coming week? For its part, Kenvue reported better-than-expected sales Friday. Away from Kenvue, we hope to get updates on how Kimberly-Clark is managing cost inflation (including on logistics); sales trends in China now that regulators have pushed back on social-media claims that its diapers contained a toxic chemical; and the outlook for its professional business in the wake of customers working down existing inventory at a faster rate than they placed new orders. Revenue: $4.13 billion EPS: $1.64 3. Jobs, jobs, jobs: This week's slate of economic data is all about the labor market. The main event is Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report, with economists expecting 75,000 payroll additions and the unemployment rate remaining at 4.2% . The jobs report arrives with inflation running well above the Fed's 2% target, potentially forcing central bankers to raise rates in the coming months after making no change at last week's policy meeting. For this reason, it's crucial that unemployment remain at bay so that the Fed has the breathing room it needs to curtail inflation. As of Friday, the CME FedWatch Tool puts the odds of a quarter-point hike at just under 75% at the December meeting. Leading up to Friday, we'll get the September JOLTS (jobs openings and labor turnover survey) report on Tuesday and ADP's October employment survey. The JOLTS report provides insight into labor market tightness by tracking job openings, hires, quits, layoffs/discharges, and other causes of separation. However, the data is a month old, and we already know the net number of jobs added to the economy in September, so it's the least consequential of the three labor-market updates. The ADP data, on the other hand, is often used by investors to game the nonfarm payrolls report, though it only covers private-sector hiring. Other economic reports to keep an eye on include the Institute for Supply Management's monthly manufacturing report, out Monday, and the Census Bureau's factory orders report, out Tuesday, both of which provide insight into the state of manufacturing. items.title: Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat escalates
items.summary: Haley Stevens, a former congresswomen who lost out on the Democratic nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, endorses his opponent days before the vote.
items.content:
A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's closely-fought US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.
Haley Stevens, a former congresswomen who lost out on the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers at a church on Sunday.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now."
"That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.
Stevens also said El-Sayed had told her she was no longer welcome in his campaign.
The pair had been scheduled to appear together at an event on Sunday, but El-Sayed reportedly asked her not to come.
They had clashed publicly over a campaign advert from a liberal group which blamed Israel for high food prices.
El-Sayed, who has not commented on Stevens's endorsement of his opponent, criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.
The Michigan Senate race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in Tuesday's midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress for the next two years.
It is one of a handful of battleground contests that will ultimately decide control of the Senate.
